newsitem.title: UK: Police investigate suspected IRA missile attack.
newsitem.headline: Police investigate suspected IRA missile attack.

text.p: Northern Ireland police said on Tuesday they were investigating a suspected IRA attack on security forces in nationalist West Belfast after two missiles were fired at an armoured vehicle.
"If would appear that something has been fired at a security forces patrol. A number of people have suffered minor cuts and shock," a police source told Reuters.

He said it seemed that two "PRIG" grenades were fired from hand-held launchers. They missed the military vehicles but it was thought they had struck some buildings. No military casualties were reported.
Propelled recoilless improvised grenades (PRIG) are a common weapon in the IRA's armoury of home-made missiles, security sources added.

The attack coincides with heightened tensions in the British province following a surge in hostilities by members of the Irish Republican Army (IRA) and revenge attacks by their pro-British Loyalist foes.
The IRA abandoned its 17-month ceasefire in a war against British rule last February, citing frustration at being kept out of British peace talks.
Since December the Irish Republican Army has stepped up activities with a spate of bomb and mortar attacks aimed at British soliders and police patrols.
Britain says the IRA must call a truce before its political wing, Sinn Fein, is given a place in multi-party discussions on the future of the province.
Northern Ireland Secretary Sir Patrick Mayhew warned on Monday that Britain would relentlessly hunt down IRA guerrillas and that they would not be allowed to bully their way into the peace talks.

"We will pursue you with every means open to us under the law," he said in a toughly worded speech. "We shall never give up. We shall go to any expense. You will never be safe." Police have blamed Loyalists for three bomb attacks on Catholic nationalists. Britain has condemned the Loyalist violence but said it believes a 28-month truce by the so-called Combined Loyalist Military Command still holds.

On Monday Northern Ireland Office junior minister Michael Ancram told reporters he did not believe politicians linked to the banned extremists had breached peace principles underpinning their places at the talks.
